# Characterization of monoclonal anti- $\beta_{2}$ -glycoprotein-I and anti-prothrombin antibody fragments generated by phage display from a patient with primary antiphospholipid syndrome

Marisol Languren a, Baltazar Becerril b, Antonio R. Cabral a, Luisa E. Fernández-Altuna a, Virginia Pascual a, Diego F. Hernández-Ramírez b, Javier Cabiedes a,\*

$^{a}$ Department of Immunology and Rheumatology, Instituto Nacional de Ciencias Médicas y Nutrición Salvador Zubirán, Vasco de Quiroga 15, 14000 Mexico City, Mexico   
$^{b}$ Department of Molecular Biology and Bioprocesses, Instituto de Biotecnología, UNAM, Cuernavaca, Morelos, Mexico

Received 23 August 2005; revised 3 October 2005; accepted 5 October 2005

# Abstract

The molecular structure of antibodies associated with autoimmune thrombosis is beginning to be understood. We describe the binding specificities and sequence analysis of anti- $\beta_{2}$ -glycoprotein-I (anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I) or anti-prothrombin (anti-PT) antibody fragments generated by phage display from a patient with primary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS). We obtained 39 positive clones, two that had the correct size reacted with $\beta_{2}$ GP-I (Beta 1 and Beta 2). Ten clones with the same restrictive pattern recognized PT (Prot 1) and cross-reacted with $\beta_{2}$ GP-I. All three clones recognized anionic and zwitterionic phospholipids. The $\mathrm{V_H}$ regions of both anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I clones are members of the VH4 family. Prot 1 has a $\mathrm{V_H}$ segment of the VH3 family. The Beta 1 $\mathrm{J_H}$ segments are $\mathrm{J_H5b}$ and $\mathrm{J_H4b}$ for Beta 2 and Prot 1. $\mathrm{V_L}$ genes are $\mathrm{V}_{\lambda}1$ , 3 and 1, respectively. No $\mathrm{J_L}$ was identified for Beta 1, while Beta 2 and Prot 1 carry $\mathrm{J}_{\lambda}3\mathrm{b}$ genes. Beta 1 and Beta 2 carry highly conserved germ-line $\mathrm{V_H}$ and $\mathrm{V_L}$ genes. Mutations of the Prot 1 gene appear to be antigen-dependent, most are hotspot mutations located in the CDR 1 and 2 regions. Our work suggests that some anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I from patients with primary APS are natural autoantibodies. Our work may also help to explain the frequent coexistence of anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I and anti-PT in the same patient.

Keywords: Phage display; scFV antibodies; Anti- $\beta_{2}$ -glycoprotein-I; Antiphospholipid syndrome

# 1. Introduction

Antiphospholipid (aPL) antibodies are the generic name of a family of autoantibodies that recognize $\beta_{2}$ -glycoprotein-I ( $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ ), prothrombin (PT), annexin V, oxidized low density lipoproteins, high molecular weight kininogen, phosphatidylserine, cardiolipin and/or phosphatidylcholine (recently reviewed in [1-3]). These antibodies are mainly found in patients with recurrent thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia or recurrent fetal loss, that is, in patients with

the antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) [4-8]. At present, it is unknown if the combinations of various aPL in the same sera confer an increased risk of thrombosis, but there is ample evidence suggesting that anti- $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ is an independent risk factor for developing thrombosis in patients with primary or secondary APS [8,9-11]. Anti-prothrombin antibodies also appear to confer an increased risk for developing thrombosis [12-14], but its clinical significance as an independent risk is still unknown [3,12].

Although significant progress has been made in the understanding of the binding specificities of anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I [15] and anti-PT [2], the molecular structure of aPL is beginning to be understood. At present, 34 antibodies (22 IgM) reactive with phospholipids or related antigens have been sequenced

<!-- page 2 -->
[16]. These antibodies were obtained from lymphocytes of healthy subjects, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with or without antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) or from patients with primary APS (recently reviewed in [16]). Of particular interest is the work of Chukwuocha et al. who studied three IgG monoclonal anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I and two anti-PT Fab fragments isolated by phage display from a patient with coronary artery disease and antibodies to oxidized low density lipoproteins [17].

Here, we report the binding specificities and sequence analysis of two antibody fragments reactive with $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ and one with PT, all generated by phage display technology from a patient with primary antiphospholipid syndrome.

# 2. Materials and methods

# 2.1. Patient

JGMA, a 25-year-old female, has an 8 years history of pulmonary embolism and classic migraine; a deep venous thrombosis of the right leg was diagnosed 6 years before study. She also had two first trimester spontaneous abortions 2 and 1 years before admission, during which times she was seen elsewhere with an elevated IgG and IgM aCL, positive lupus anticoagulant and an acquired activated protein C resistance. At the time of admission at our Institute she had elevated IgG and IgM aCL and positive lupus anticoagulant (Russell viper venom). Her serum anti-DNA (ELISA) and anti-nuclear antibodies (HEp-2 cells) were negative. Patient had neither history of arthritis, malar rash nor renal involvement. She was diagnosed as having PAPS [4]. After a follow up for 24 months, JMGA has remained essentially asymptomatic on oral anticoagulants despite having persistently elevated IgG aCL, IgM aCL and IgG anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I. At time of study patient had elevated serum IgG and IgM anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I and aCL [4].

# 2.2. Construction of scFV libraries

$\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ and $\mathrm{V_LJ_L}$ genomic libraries were constructed according to published methods [18,19]. In brief, mononuclear cells were used as source of total RNA [20] to generate phage library. We used PCR to amplify the $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ , $\mathrm{V_LJ_L}$ ( $\kappa$ and $\lambda$ ) and the linker to subsequently assemble them by overlapping PCR to generate the scFV fragments. These fragments were then ligated to the phagemid vector pSyn 2 to transform electrocompetent Escherichia coli XL-1 blue strain (Gibco). Phages were purified by polyethylene-glycol precipitation and the specific scFV fragments were selected by their binding to $\beta_{2}$ -glycoprotein-I or prothrombin bound to propylene tubes as described in the next section.

# 2.3. Selection of anti- $\beta_{2}$ -glycoprotein-I or anti-prothrombin clones

This was done according to published methods [21]. Briefly, we incubated human $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ $(25\mu \mathrm{g / ml})$ purified in our laboratory [22] or human prothrombin $(25\mu \mathrm{g / ml}$ Sigma, St.

Louis, Missouri), both in PBS, in $12 \times 75 \mathrm{~mm}$ polystyrene test tubes (Falcon) overnight at room temperature. Tubes were then blocked with $2 \%$ powder milk in PBS containing $0.01 \%$ Tween 20 for $2 \mathrm{~h}$ at room temperature, after which $10^{13}$ unit forming colonies containing surface phage-scFVs were incubated for an hour at $37^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ . After three washes with $0.05 \%$ Tween 20 in PBS, phage-scFVs were eluted with $0.2 \mathrm{M}$ glycine-HCl buffer, pH 2.2 and $1 \mathrm{M}$ Trizma-base pH 9.1. This binding/elution cycle was repeated four times. Phage-scFVs were titered twice per cycle to evaluate the efficiency of the system. Similarly, in each round the concentration of the antigens was reduced by half (last $1.6 \mu \mathrm{g} / \mathrm{ml}$ ) to select the high affinity phage-scFVs. After the fourth round of selection the isolated clones were grown in 96-well culture plates (97F, Nunc Inc, Denmark) with YT2X culture medium supplemented with $2 \%$ glucose and ampicillin $(200 \mu \mathrm{g} / \mathrm{ml})$ , tetracycline $(12.5 \mu \mathrm{g} / \mathrm{ml})$ . When cultures reached 0.7 optical densities (OD) we infected them with the M13/K07 helper phage to obtain phage-antibody particles. We utilized the culture supernatants to determine their specificities by ELISA.

# 2.4. Anti- $\beta_{2}GP - I$ and anti-PT ELISA

We coated non-irradiated microtiter plates (Nunc-Immunoplate II, Nunc, Denmark) with $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ or PT (both at $10~\mu \mathrm{g}/$ ml) according to previously published methods [10]. We incubated $1\times 10^{9}$ phage-scFVs for $1\textrm{h}$ at $37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and after three washes with PBS at RT a peroxidase conjugated anti-M13 antibody (Amersham Pharmacia Biotech) was added for an additional hour at $37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Color was developed with $0.01\%$ $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2$ o-phenylendiamine in citrate buffer pH 5.0. After $1\textrm{h}$ at $37^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ the reaction was stopped with $5\mathrm{M}\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$ . Absorbance was read at $490\mathrm{nm}$ in an ELISA reader (TECAN).

# 2.5. Anti-phospholipid ELISA

The reactivity of the clones against the following $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ free antigens (all from Sigma) was also studied by ELISA [10]: cardiolipin (CL), phosphatidylglycerol (PTG), phosphatidylinositol (PTI), phosphatidylserine (PTS), sphingomyelin (SM), phosphatidylcholine (PTC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PTE) and phosphatidic acid (PA).

# 2.6. ELISA for phylogenetically conserved antigens

We also studied the reactivity of the scFV fragments against vimentin, aggregated gammaglobulin (all from Sigma) according to methods developed in our laboratory.

# 2.7. Nuclear or cytoplasmic antigens present in HEp-2 cells

These were determined by immunofluorescence according to standard methods.

<!-- page 3 -->
# 2.8. Gene sequencing

The $\mathrm{V_HD_JH}$ linker- $\mathrm{V_LJ_L}$ rearrangements were sequenced in an ABI prisma 377 PE automated sequencer (Applied Biosystems). We used the Lmb3 and pCANTAB5B-S6 oligonucleotides according to published methods [19]. The resulting sequences were analyzed with the V Base data base (available in www.wd.mrc-cpe.cam.ac.uk/vbase).

# 2.9. Analysis of the number and distribution of somatic mutations

The distribution of the replacement and silent mutations was analyzed by the multinomial method proposed by Lossos et al. [23]. A $p$ value of $< 0.05$ for the framework (FR) or complementarity regions (CDR) for the heavy or light chains favors that the mutations are antigen-dependent [16].

# 2.10. Analysis of mutational hotspots

We identified the mutational hotspots by the hotspot consensus sequence RGYW, its complementary sequence WRCY (where $\mathbf{R} =$ purine, $\mathrm{Y} =$ pyrimidine and $\mathrm{W} = \mathrm{A}$ or T) and by the highly mutable trinucleotides (AGC, GCT, ATT, AAT, TAC GTA, AGT and AGA), most of which are part of the RGYW/WRCY motif [24,25].

# 3. Results

After the amplification of the $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ , $\mathrm{V_LJ_L}$ rearrangements and the linker sequence, we assembled them by means of an overlapping PCR to obtain the single chain variable format fragments (scFV). We then ligated these fragments to the phagemid vector pSyn 2 to transform the electrocompetent $E$ . coli XL1-blue strain. A random analysis of 20 clones of the $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ -linker- $\mathrm{V_KJ_K}$ showed that 17/20 (85%) had the right size, two were single chains ( $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ or $\mathrm{V_LJ_L}$ ) and the other was the linker alone. Of the remaining 17 clones we obtained 15 that had different digestion patterns with the frequent cut enzyme BstNI, but one of them repeated once. The $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ -linker- $\mathrm{V}_\lambda \mathrm{J}_\lambda$ library showed that 16/20 (80%) had the right size but with different digestion patterns. The sequence analysis showed that they belong to the following families: VH1, VH3, VH4, VH5 and VH6 and have the genes JH-1, JH-3, JH4, JH5 and JH6 with the rearrangements $\mathrm{V}_\lambda 2$ , $\mathrm{V}_\lambda 3\mathrm{a}$ , $\mathrm{V}_\kappa 1$ , $\mathrm{V}_\kappa 3$ , $\mathrm{V}_\kappa 4$ and $\mathrm{V}_\kappa 6$ .

Table 1 shows the results of anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I or anti-prothrombin clones after the selection process. It can be seen that the number of clones was reduced in every round because we reduced by half the concentration of the antigens and increased the astringency of buffers in every cycle. After the fourth round of selection of the $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ -linker- $\mathrm{V}_{\kappa} \mathrm{J}_{\kappa}$ and $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H}$ -linker- $\mathrm{V}_{\lambda} \mathrm{J}_{\lambda}$ libraries, we randomly selected 88 clones, propagated them and studied their reactivity by ELISA. # 3.2. Anti-prothrombin activity

Of the 88 clones obtained after the fourth round of selection, 38 recognized PT, but only 10 had the right size and the same restrictive pattern (Fig. 3); all reacted with prothrombin (Fig. 2). This is the Prot 1 clone. Interestingly, Prot 1 cross-reacted with $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ (Fig. 2).

# 3.3. Sequence analysis

# 3.3.1. Beta 1 clone

This clone has a $\mathrm{V_H}$ region which is a member of the $\mathrm{V_H4}$ family. Fig. 4a shows that this rearrangement has $97\%$ homology with the germ-line gene VHSP/VH4.22...+. The disparity is in 10 bp substitutions (three transitions, seven transversions and one unidentified base) located in $\mathrm{FW1} = 5$ , $\mathrm{FW2} = 1$ , $\mathrm{FW3} = 3$ and $\mathrm{CDR2} = 1$ regions (Fig. 4a). The $\mathrm{V_H}$ segment is rearranged with the $\mathrm{J_H5b}$ gene that has a homology of $98\%$ . We did not identify a D gene. The $\mathrm{V_L}$ gene is

# 3.3.3. Prot 1 clone

The $\mathrm{V_H}$ region of Prot 1 is a member of the $\mathrm{V_H3}$ family. In Fig. 6a we show that this gene has $98.6\%$ homology with the germ-line gene DP-47/V3-23 with four mutations located in $\mathrm{FW1} = 2$ , $\mathrm{FW3} = 2$ (one transition and three transversions). This $\mathrm{V_H}$ segment has $83\%$ homology with the $\mathrm{J_H4b}$ gene. No D gene was identified. Prot 1 is rearranged with the $\mathrm{V_L}$ 1b.366F5/DPL5...+ gene product that belongs to the $\mathrm{V}_{\lambda}1$ family with a homology of $93.5\%$ due to 19 mutations of 294 bases (10 transitions and nine transversions) located in $\mathrm{FW1} = 1$ , $\mathrm{CDR1} = 4$ , $\mathrm{FW2} = 2$ , $\mathrm{CDR2} = 4$ and $\mathrm{FW3} = 8$ . This $\mathrm{V_L}$ segment is rearranged with the $\mathrm{J}_{\lambda}3\mathrm{b}$ gene product that has $86.6\%$ homology due to four mutations in 30 bases (Fig. 6b).

Table 2 shows a summary of the genetic origins of Beta 1, Beta 2 and Prot 1 clones.

# 3.3.4. Amino acid substitutions

The number of mutations in the heavy and light chains in Beta 1, Beta 2 and Prot 1 that resulted in replacement of

arginine, lysine (cationic) or asparagine (partially charged) are shown in Table 3.

# 3.3.5. Statistical comparison of the clone gene sequences with germ-line genes

In Table 4 we show that the mutations found in the rearrangements of Beta 1 and Beta 2 clones of heavy chains and those of the light chain of the Beta 2 clone are not statistically different from their respective germ-line genes. The multinomial analysis of the FR mutations of the heavy chain of Prot 1 suggests that these are antigen-dependent $(p < 0.001)$ and to a lesser extent, but still statistically significant, those of the FR region of the light chain $(p = 0.01)$ (Table 4).

# 3.3.6. Location of the hotspot mutations

All three clones have 23 mutational hotspots (three silent); these are mostly distributed in the $\mathrm{V_LJ_L}$ chains of Beta 2 and Prot 1 clones. Nine mutations are within the consensus sequence RGYW (Pu-G-Py-A/T) or its complementary one WRCY, five in the highly mutable trinucleotide AGC and three in AGA; the sequences ATT, TAC, AAT, GTA and AAT are equally represented. Only 7/23 $(30\%)$ of the mutational hot-spots are located in the CDR regions, this corresponds to $54\%$ of the mutations $(n = 13)$ found in these regions. It is

# 3.3.7. Reactivity against phospholipids

Fig. 7 shows the reactivity of our three clones with eight phospholipids: four negatively charged (CL, PTS, PTI, and PTG) and four zwitterionic (PTC, PTE, SM and PA). As can be seen, all antigens were heterogeneously recognized by the three clones.

# 3.3.8. Reactivity against phylogenetically conserved antigens

No clone reacted with dsDNA, ssDNA, vimentin, aggregated gammaglobulin, nuclear or cytoplasmic antigens present in HEp-2 cells (Table 6).

# 4. Discussion

We generated two cDNA libraries with the $\mathrm{V_HD_JH / V_KJ_K}$ and $\mathrm{V_HDJ_H / V_\lambda J_\lambda}$ rearrangements, respectively, both expressed as scFV on the surface of the M13 phage as fusion proteins linked to the pIII phage protein. To expedite the process we

mixed both libraries and purified the clones reactive with $\beta_{2}$ -glycoprotein-I or prothrombin. After the fourth round of selection under astringent conditions, we obtained three clones: two reacted with $\beta_{2}$ GP-I (Beta 1 and Beta 2) and one recognized prothrombin (Prot 1). Both anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I clones showed to carry $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{H}}4$ genes with 97 and $99\%$ structural homology with germ-line genes, $\mathrm{J}_{\mathrm{H}}5\mathrm{b}$ and $\mathrm{J}_{\mathrm{H}}4\mathrm{b}$ genes, with 98 and $82.3\%$ homology, and $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ genes of the $\mathrm{V}_{\lambda}1$ and $\mathrm{V}_{\lambda}3$ families are 99.6 and $88.88\%$ homologous with their germ-line genes. The $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ segment of the Beta 2 clone is rearranged with the product of the $\mathrm{J}_{\lambda}3\mathrm{b}$ gene with a homology of $93.3\%$ . Clone Prot 1 carries a gene of the $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{H}}3$ family with a homology of $98.6\%$ and is rearranged with the product of the $\mathrm{J}_{\mathrm{H}}4\mathrm{b}$ gene (homology $83.3\%$ ). This sequence, rearranged with the gene 1b.366F5/DPL5...+ of the $\mathrm{V}_{\lambda}1$ family, has a homology of $93.5\%$ and is rearranged with the $\mathrm{J}_{\lambda}3\mathrm{b}$ gene (homology of $86.6\%$ ). The multinomial analysis of the distribution of the replacement and silent mutations compared with their respective germ-line genes suggests that those present in Beta 1 and Beta 2 clones are piggy-backed mutations while those of Prot 1 appear to be antigen-driven [23]. This is in line with our findings that most mutational intrinsic hotspots found in Beta 1 and Beta 2 clones are located in framework regions while those present in Prot 1 clustered preferentially in CDRs [24,25].

One previous study utilized the same phage display technology used in our work to generate anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I antibodies in scFV format [17]. Chukwuocha et al. obtained cDNA from peripheral mononuclear cells from a patient with coronary heart disease, positive anti-oxidized low density lipoprotein antibodies, and no thrombotic manifestations. Therefore, ours is the first study of autoantibodies to $\beta_{2}$ GP-I and PT in scFV format from a patient with primary antiphospholipid syndrome. anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I and two anti-PT [17]. These authors found that two anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I and one anti-PT shared identical $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{H}}6$ -D- $\mathrm{J}_{\mathrm{H}}$ but different L rearrangements; the other anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I had $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{H}}26 / \mathrm{V}3 - 23$ segments while the second anti-PT had the $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{H}}4.33$ segment [17]. Sequence analysis of both autoantibodies showed a structural homology of 92 and $98\%$ with germline genes [17]. In a subsequent multinomial analysis, Giles et al. reported that the gene mutations, except one from an anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I, were not induced by antigen [16]. These findings, together with those reported here, suggest that the anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I specificity appears not to be dependent of antigen selection. These results, however, should be taken with caution since

the phage display methodology generates monoclonal antibody fragments with $\mathrm{V_H} / \mathrm{V_L}$ gene combinations that may not represent the anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I detected in patients' sera [26]. It is nevertheless important to note that the genetic origins of the scFV fragments thus far reported [17] including ours are similar to those found in antiphospholipid antibodies from APS patients studied by conventional techniques [16]. It is also noteworthy that the heavy and light chains of anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I and anti-PT reported here are those utilized by some autoantibodies with different specificities, i.e., rheumatoid factor and anti-DNA [27,28].

As stated before, clone Prot 1 has mutations that appear to be antigen-driven [23]. It is interesting that Prot 1 cross-reacted with $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ in spite that the antigen used to select it was prothrombin. This crossreactivity is similar to one of Chukwocha's clones [17]. Prot 1 is also the clone that accumulated more cationic amino acids such as arginine, lysine or partially charged residues as asparagine in the $\mathrm{V_H}$ region. These findings may thus help to explain, at least in part, the cross-reactivity of anti-PT with $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ , which, as known, is a protein that contains several negatively charged regions [29]. It is unknown if the epitope present in prothrombin is anionic, but it is unlikely in view that we used highly astringent in vitro conditions to select Prot 1. To identify the shared epitope it will be necessary to first identify the epitope recognized by Prot 1 and then screen $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ peptide libraries. These studies will have practical and pathogenetic importance since it is known that anti-PT and anti- $\beta_{2}\mathrm{GP - I}$ almost uniformly coexist in the serum of patients with primary or secondary antiphospholipid syndromes [30].

Our work also showed that the scFV fragments reacted with cationic and zwitterionic phospholipids, but not with evolutionary conserved antigens, suggesting that the epitope may reside in the fatty acid chains and/or the glycerol-phosphate moiety. This is a characteristic of human oligoreactive natural autoantibodies [31,32]. This finding together with the fact that anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I are coded by germ-line genes may have pathogenetic relevance since it was not known that anti- $\beta_{2}$ GP-I from patients with primary APS belong to the family of natural autoantibodies [31-33].
